text: They agree more than their titles suggest: LoRA matches full fine-tuning when the data fits in its capacity and it is set up right, and falls behind when the data is pretraining-sized. "LoRA learns less and forgets less" (Biderman et al., 2024) Biderman et al. trained Llama-2-7B on code and on math, two ways each: continued pretraining (CPT: StarCoder-Python up to 20B tokens; OpenWebMath, 14.7B tokens) and instruction fine-tuning (IFT: Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K, 73M tokens; MetaMathQA, 103M tokens).
label: core
key: falls behind when the data is pretraining-sized

text: The two studies, reconciled Biderman et al.'s continued pretraining runs (14.7 to 20B tokens) are exactly the "datasets that exceed LoRA capacity" regime; their instruction runs, where LoRA caught up, are the "low-regret" regime.

text: Thinking Machines cites them for this: LoRA underperforms "in settings that resemble pre-training".

text: Use full fine-tuning or continued pretraining for billions of tokens of new domain text; LoRA for post-training.

text: A worked instance at the small end A Qwen 3.8 4B model was taught to write PostgreSQL query plans: SFT on 400 GPT-6 Astra trajectories (440 generated in two rounds of 120 and 320, each keeping 20 for validation) through a LoRA of 21.2 million parameters (42.5 MB), then a custom "anchored" GRPO against measured execution time.
label: depth

text: Best of three rollouts, it reached a 1.81 times geometric-mean speed-up over Postgres's own planner on 113 join-heavy queries, for $1,200 in total (about $800 of rented 2 × H100 time and $400 of API fees; development on two RTX 3090s) ( write-up, 16 September 2026 ).

text: QLoRA: LoRA on a 4-bit base QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) stores the frozen base in 4 bits and trains bf16 LoRA adapters on top, backpropagating through the dequantised weights.
label: core
key: QLoRA backpropagates through the dequantised 4-bit weights into bf16 adapters

text: That took fine-tuning a 65B model from more than 780 GB of GPU memory to under 48 GB, one GPU, "without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline".
label: core
key: "without degrading the runtime or predictive performance

text: Three pieces: 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) : a 16-value code whose levels follow a normal distribution, since pretrained weights roughly do; blocks of 64 weights share one scale.
label: core
key: a 16-value code whose levels follow a normal distribution

text: The paper calls it "information theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights"; Yoshida (2023) shows it cannot quite be, because the distribution of the scaled values depends on the block size.
label: core

text: The QLoRA page builds the code and measures it on real LLaMA weights.
label: core
key: built and measured on real LLaMA weights

text: Double quantisation : the per-block scales are themselves quantised, saving about 0.37 bits per parameter (about 3 GB on a 65B model).
label: core

text: Paged optimizers : optimizer state in NVIDIA unified memory, so a long batch's memory spike pages to CPU instead of crashing.
label: core
key: pages to CPU instead of crashing

text: QLoRA's recipe put LoRA on every linear layer (r = 64, α = 16).
label: core

text: The trade is time: Sebastian Raschka measured 33% less memory for 39% more training time (21.33 GB and 1.85 h with bf16 LoRA against 14.18 GB and 2.79 h with QLoRA, in one of his runs) ( Practical tips ).
label: core

text: The adapter was trained against the dequantised 4-bit weights, so its product is right relative to those.
label: core
key: its product is right relative to those

text: The usual routes: merge into the original 16-bit weights and quantise the result again (which adds a fresh rounding error); keep the adapter separate at serving time; or train so the merge stays quantised, as QA-LoRA does.
label: core

text: Some formats cannot merge at all: the PEFT docs say adapters on AQLM-quantised models "shall be saved separately, as merging them with AQLM quantized weights is not possible" ( PEFT quantization guide ).
label: core

text: LoftQ goes the other way, choosing the LoRA initialisation to cancel part of the quantisation error.
label: core

text: DoRA: magnitude and direction DoRA (Liu et al., ICML 2024) splits each weight column into a length and a direction, trains the length directly and the direction with LoRA: W′ = m · (W 0 + BA) / ‖W 0 + BA‖ c m a trainable magnitude vector, one number per column (per output unit in PyTorch's layout), initialised to ‖W 0 ‖ c ‖·‖ c "the vector-wise norm of a matrix across each column vector" The motivation is an analysis of how fine-tuning changes each column.
label: core
key: the vector-wise norm of a matrix across each column vector

text: In the paper's measurements, full fine-tuning's changes in magnitude and in direction were negatively correlated across checkpoints (a large turn with a small stretch, or the reverse) while LoRA's were positively correlated: one low-rank update moves both together.
label: core

text: To save memory DoRA treats the norm as a constant in the backward pass, which cut training memory by about 24.4% on LLaMA with a 0.2-point difference in accuracy.

text: S-LoRA ( Sheng et al. ) keeps every adapter in host memory, fetches the ones the running requests need, and pages adapter weights and the KV cache from one memory pool ("Unified Paging"), with kernels that batch requests for adapters of different ranks.
label: core

text: It served 2,000 adapters on one GPU at 7.61 requests per second, against 8.05 with five.
label: core

text: The baseline that merges each adapter into its own copy ran out of memory beyond a handful, and was 4 times slower even then: derived 8.05 / 2.04 = 3.9 times, and 7.99 / 0.25 = 32 times faster than PEFT, which swaps adapters between batches.
label: core

text: Punica ( Chen et al. ) introduced the batching kernel for different LoRA models against one copy of the base: 12 times the throughput of then state-of-the-art serving systems, adding 2 ms of latency per token.
